human_tolerance.notes: Present in heavily wooded suburban regions but never in large numbers there, so a wooded lot with mature hickory, beech, maple or oak suits it. Takes nest boxes readily and can be hand-fed, which is how most people meet it.

phases.name: breeding
phases.note: The main breeding season; two litters a year are produced in both the wild and captivity, and the southern populations breed later in spring than the northern ones.

phases.name: young
phases.note: Gestation is about 40 days; kits are born furless and helpless, the ears open at 2-6 days, fur grows in by 7, the eyes open at 24-30 days, they are weaned at about 65 days and are independent at around 120 days.

phases.name: caching
phases.note: Acorns and other nuts are cached, especially for winter; stored food is recovered by spatial memory in dry substrate and by smell once it is wet.

phases.name: flocking
phases.note: Winter communal nesting: animals aggregate in cavities as temperatures decline, and squirrels in aggregates save about 30% more energy than solitary nesters.

phases.name: nesting
phases.note: Two litters a year, of two to seven young; mothers wean the young 65 days after they are born. Cavities are used for breeding and, more intensively, in winter, while leaf nests serve mainly as summer refuges.

vocalizations.description: A short, sharp 'kuk' bark given when the animal is disturbed or discovers a predator, and used in confrontations between adults; often repeated in a series.
A drawn-out, high-pitched squeal of alarm and distress, the loudest and most far-carrying call in the repertoire of a species that is mostly active after dark.
A low, soft clucking or chuckling call used between individuals sharing a nest or a foraging tree, and by a mother calling her kits.
A soft, low murmuring chatter used between pairs at a nest or a feeding tree, most often heard after dark.

external.note: GBIF usage key 2437338 from the GBIF backbone match; NCBI taxon id via Wikidata P685.

conservation.note: Wikidata P141 = least concern (Q211005). The IUCN Red List page itself is not openly licensed, so it is not cited.

range.note: Wikipedia's lead: 'found in deciduous and mixed woods in the eastern half of North America, from southeastern Canada to Florida. Disjunct populations of this species have been recorded in the highlands of Mexico, Guatemala, and Honduras.' The country list follows that statement.

traits.locomotion_modes.note: The Gliding section describes launching from a tree, spreading the patagium and steering a glide, and adds that the animal is 'very clumsy walkers' and will hide rather than run when caught on the ground. The schema's Walk and Climb are the modes that map onto the block plan; the glide is carried by traits.flight instead, because the quadruped plan has no glide pose.

traits.flight.note: 'Flying squirrels do not actually fly, but rather glide using a membrane called a patagium' - hence Glide, not Powered.

traits.nest_type.note: Wikipedia's Habitat section: the species 'nest[s] in natural cavities and woodpecker holes, or build[s] nest out of leaves and twigs. Leaf nests are used as a refuge or a resting site ... whereas cavities are used for breeding and more intensively during winter.' Cavity is the primary type and the leaf nest is covered under habitat.resources as leaf_litter.

traits.perching.note: Sits on branches and climbs trunks, but does not grip a perch with its feet the way a bird does; set to false.

traits.size_class.note: From mass_kg: 71.9 g falls in the schema's 'Small' band (below 1 kg).

traits.mass_kg.note: PanTHERIA AdultBodyMass_g 71.90 g. Wikipedia gives no body mass for this species, so the dataset value is used unchanged; it sits inside the 60-110 g band that the genus's other members occupy.

traits.mass_range_kg.note: Authored band around the PanTHERIA mean: 60-110 g. No open source gives a mass range for this species, so this is a judgement envelope consistent with a 71.9 g species mean and with the size variation reported across the 11 recognised subspecies.

traits.length_m.note: Midpoint of Wikipedia's 'Total length (including tail) is 21-26 cm', i.e. 23.5 cm. PanTHERIA AdultHeadBodyLen_mm 127.98 mm is consistent once the 8-12 cm flattened tail is added.

traits.shoulder_height_m.note: Judgement: no open source gives a standing/shoulder height for this species. Estimated at 3.5 cm from a 12.8 cm head-body length (PanTHERIA) and the very low build of a gliding squirrel; the same convention as apodemus-sylvaticus in this repository.

traits.lifespan_y.note: PanTHERIA MaxLongevity_m 144 months, i.e. 12 years, taken as the documented maximum rather than a typical wild lifespan. Wikipedia gives no lifespan figure for this species.

traits.home_range_ha.note: Wikipedia's Habitat section lists three published average home-range estimates for adult males - 2.45 ha, 9 ha and 16 ha - and 1.95, 3.9 and 7.2 ha for adult females. The smallest published male mean (2.45 ha) is used, being the least demanding published figure for the species.

traits.diet.note: Wikipedia's Description and ecology section: 'feed on fruits and nuts from trees such as red and white oak, hickory, and beech. They store food, especially acorns, for winter consumption. They also dine on insects, buds, mushrooms, mycorrhizal fungi, carrion, bird eggs, nestlings, and flowers.' Mast takes half the diet because the caching behaviour described under Behavior is acorn-led and the nest trees named are oaks and hickories; fruit covers fruits and mushrooms; browse covers buds and flowers; invertebrate covers insects. The vertebrate and carrion shares (bird eggs, nestlings and carrion) are deliberately small: the same sentence presents them as opportunistic extras to a largely plant diet, and no open source weights them.

traits.social.note: Wikipedia's Behavior section: the species is 'highly social ... observed flying and foraging together in large groups', aggregates in dens as temperatures decline, and Layne and Raymond 'discovered that the southern populations also nest in large groups (up to 25 individuals)'. Group size 1-25 covers solitary summer foragers and the largest winter aggregation reported.

traits.activity_pattern.note: 'They are nocturnal and feed on fruits and nuts from trees such as red and white oak, hickory, and beech.'

traits.defense.note: Wikipedia's Gliding section: after landing the squirrel runs round the far side of the trunk or up the tree to avoid predators, and 'if they happen to be on the ground in the presence of danger, they will prefer to hide rather than attempt to escape'. Hide is the schema's closer value; the glide itself is the escape, so the ground response is concealment.

traits.wariness.note: Judgement: above mid-range, because the animal is nocturnal, small and taken by snakes, owls, hawks, raccoons and domestic cats, all of which Wikipedia lists as its predators.

habitat.use.note: PanTHERIA Terrestriality 2.00 (arboreal) sets the primary stratum, and the whole of Wikipedia's Habitat and Gliding sections describe canopy and cavity use; the small ground share reflects only the animal's clumsy walking.

habitat.shelter_tag.note: Roosts in tree cavities in winter and in leaf nests in summer.

habitat.resources.note: Food weights follow traits.diet. The cavity and leaf_litter shelter weights follow Wikipedia's statement that cavities are used for breeding and more intensively in winter while leaf nests are chiefly a summer refuge.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: Wikipedia's Habitat section: 'Although southern flying squirrels may be present in heavily wooded suburban regions, they never occur in large numbers in these areas' - hence Adapter rather than Exploiter, with uses_gardens true because the habitat features named (large hickory and beech, maple, poplar and oak) are ordinary garden-canopy trees.

habitat.density_per_ha.note: Typical from PanTHERIA PopulationDensity_n/km2 447.59 converted to 4.48 per hectare; min and max are an authored tenfold band either side, following the same convention used for sciurus-carolinensis and vulpes-vulpes.

seasonal.strategy.note: The animal is active year round; communal nesting in winter is an energy-saving behaviour, not dormancy, and no source describes hibernation.

seasonal.phases.note: Gestation, the two litters a year, the sequence of kit development (ears 2-6 days, fur by 7, eyes 24-30, weaning at 65 days, independence at about 120) and the 30% energy saving from winter aggregation are all from Wikipedia's Description and ecology and Behavior sections. The month windows attached to them are authored, since Wikipedia dates the breeding season only by saying southern populations breed later in spring than northern ones. The caching window is judgement, tied to the autumn nut crop.

seasonal.life_stages.note: Juvenile duration 120 days is Wikipedia's stated age of independence; scale 0.6 is authored judgement for a small mammal whose eyes do not open until 24-30 days.

vocalizations.note: Wikipedia describes this species as rarely vocal and gives no account of its calls, so the three entries here are the standard sciurid repertoire (kuk, squeal, cluck) authored by analogy with the closely related sciurus-carolinensis record in this repository and with published accounts of flying squirrel vocalisation. Descriptions, contexts, night time windows and cooldowns are all authored judgement; no open source found quantifies them, and no frequency bands are given, so freq_hz is omitted.

look.note: Palette follows Wikipedia's Description and ecology section: 'grey-brown fur on top with darker flanks and a cream colored underneath ... large dark eyes and flattened tails', with the patagium membrane and the darker dorsal line drawn as extra_parts because the quadruped plan has no membrane part. Proportions are authored judgement, with a long flattened tail and a big head for the genus.

behavior.note: Authored parameters for the shared ground-forager program. The program's default rest window (10 to 90 degrees) is kept because its description gives that as the setting for nocturnal and crepuscular species. food_tag mast follows the largest diet fraction; flee and food radii are judgement, scaled down from the fox example for a 72 g animal. The program is shared rather than bespoke because the foraging loop it describes - seek food, flee a threat, return to shelter - is the animal's, but its glide has no pose in the quadruped plan and is not animated here.

vocalizations.chatter.note: No allow-listed open source describes this species' calls. The entry exists so the record can carry a nocturnal call at all, and its wording, time window and cooldown are authored, not sourced.
